Menopause weight gain isn’t a willpower problem. Your scale can barely move while your body changes underneath it: more fat around your organs, less muscle, and an appetite system working against you. A review published in September in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences pulls together 25 years of research on what falling estrogen does to appetite. Estrogen helps run the hunger switch in the hypothalamus; when it falls, the balance tips toward hunger. Leptin, the hormone that tells your brain you’ve had enough, rises, but the brain responds to it less. Ghrelin, your hunger hormone, dips after a meal but climbs back faster. The menopause guideline most OB-GYNs have practiced under was written in 2014, before the newest nonhormonal drugs existed and before the FDA changed the hormone therapy label. On October 15, ACOG replaced it: Clinical Practice Guideline No. 13, published in Obstetrics & Gynecology (2026), covering hot flushes, sleep, and mood. Hormone therapy is strongly recommended for hot flushes and the sleep disruption they cause, started before 60 or within 10 years of menopause; continuing past 60 may be necessary if symptoms persist. Perimenopause raises psychological symptom burden 52%. And it's not what you think. A new peer-reviewed study of 7,975 women across 20 countries measured it on the Menopause Rating Scale: 7.3 in perimenopause versus 4.8 in premenopause. We assume that load is anxiety and depression. It isn't. The single largest jump was exhaustion, up 56%, followed by irritability. Depressive mood and anxiety rose too, but they were the smallest movers, not the headline. And this is the part most coverage skips: the increase held after adjusting for age, education, income, ethnicity, BMI, smoking, alcohol, and an existing diagnosis of anxiety or depression.
